title: How to Clean and Seal Driveway Cracks Before Winter (Concrete and Asphalt)
question: There are cracks forming in my driveway and winter is coming — how do I clean and seal them so water and freezing don't make them worse?
summary: Sealing cracks before winter keeps water out, so freeze-thaw can't pry them wider each cold snap. The most common mistake is using the wrong filler for the job: a thin, pourable liquid runs straight through a wide crack, and asphalt filler and concrete sealant are not interchangeable. Match the product to both the surface (rigid gray concrete vs. flexible black asphalt) and the crack width, clean and dry the crack fully first, and work in a dry, above-50°F window. A crack with a vertical step (one side higher than the other) or that keeps returning yearly is a base/structural problem, not a caulk problem — that one needs a pro.

commonCauses.cause: Water sitting in existing cracks then freezing and thawing, which pries them wider each winter
commonCauses.quickCheck: Compare a crack to last year — if it's noticeably wider, has crumbling/spalling edges, or holds water after rain, freeze-thaw is enlarging it.

commonCauses.cause: Normal concrete shrinkage as the slab cured (hairline and control-joint cracks)
commonCauses.quickCheck: Look for thin hairline cracks that run in a fairly straight line or from a control joint, sit flat with no step, and haven't grown much over time.

commonCauses.cause: Ground settling or a weak/eroded base under the slab
commonCauses.quickCheck: Lay a straightedge across the crack — if one side is lower than the other (a vertical step), or the crack is near a downspout or driveway edge, the base is moving.

commonCauses.cause: Asphalt aging and drying out (oxidation), losing its flexible binder
commonCauses.quickCheck: On asphalt, check for a gray, faded, brittle surface with loose aggregate (raveling) or interconnected 'alligator' cracking — signs the binder has dried out.

commonCauses.cause: Tree roots growing under and lifting the slab
commonCauses.quickCheck: See if the crack is near a tree and the pavement is heaved up (higher, not sunken) along a line pointing back toward the trunk.

fixes: Pick the right weather window: at least 2-3 dry days with daytime temps above about 50°F and no rain or hard freeze forecast for 24-48 hours after. Early fall, before the first freezes, is ideal — sealing in spring/summer heat also works.

Walk the driveway and sort the cracks. Measure each width (hairline, up to 1/4 inch, 1/4 to 1/2 inch, or over 1/2 inch) and note the surface: concrete (rigid, gray) or asphalt (flexible, black). You'll pick different products for each.

Flag the ones you should NOT DIY: any crack with a vertical step between sides, a slab that's visibly sunken or tilting, or wide interconnected 'alligator' areas. Stop on those and get a pro — filling them only hides base failure.

Clean each crack thoroughly. Pull weeds, dig out loose debris with a screwdriver, chisel out crumbling edges, then wire-brush and blow it clean with compressed air, a leaf blower, or a shop vac. Degrease oily asphalt spots. The crack must end up clean and fully dry — filler will not bond to dirt, moisture, or loose material. (Chiseling or grinding concrete makes silica dust — see the safety note before you cut.)

For deep or wide cracks (roughly over 1/2 inch deep or 1/4 inch wide), press foam backer rod into the crack so the sealant sits on top instead of sinking away. Set it so you fill the top 1/4 to 1/2 inch. Sand can back up very deep cracks under a top layer of sealant.

Choose the correct filler. Concrete: use a masonry/concrete crack sealant — a self-leveling polyurethane for cracks up to ~1/2 inch, or a trowel-grade concrete patch for wider ones. Asphalt: use an asphalt crack filler — a pourable cold rubberized-emulsion bottle for thin cracks, or a trowel-grade cold filler for wider ones. (Hot-applied crack sealant lasts longer but needs a melter and runs 300°F+ — that's an advanced/pro method with real burn risk; a homeowner should default to cold-pour.) Do not put asphalt filler in concrete or vice versa; they're formulated for different movement.

Apply the filler. Cut the nozzle to match the crack width and fill flush to slightly proud of the surface. Self-leveling products spread themselves flat; overfill asphalt filler a little because it shrinks as it cures. Tool it smooth with a putty knife or trowel.
Let it cure fully per the product label (a few hours to 24-48 hours) before driving or parking on it, and keep it dry during cure. Rushing traffic onto uncured filler tears the seal.

Optional, asphalt only: once crack repairs have cured, apply a driveway sealcoat with a squeegee/brush to protect the whole surface and blend the repairs. Never sealcoat concrete — it doesn't take it (use a penetrating concrete sealer if you want to seal concrete). Do this on a dry, mild day.
Re-inspect next fall. Crack fillers shrink and weather, so top off any that dropped or reopened. Yearly touch-ups are normal and are what keep small cracks from turning into base failure.
diyVsPro: DIY is fine for surface cracks up to about 1/2 inch wide on a slab that's still flat and stable — cleaning, filling, and sealing them is standard homeowner maintenance. Stop and call a licensed concrete or paving contractor when: a crack is wider than roughly 1/2 to 3/4 inch; there's a vertical step where one side sits higher/lower than the other (settling or heaving); the slab is visibly sunken, tilting, or rocking; there are large interconnected 'alligator' cracked areas; cracks radiate from a low spot or keep coming back every year (the base has failed); or heaving is coming from tree roots. Those need real repair — mudjacking/foam leveling, base rework, or slab/section replacement — not filler. Hot-applied asphalt crack sealing is also best left to a paver.
typicalCostUSD: DIY: about $15-60 for a few tubes/bottles of crack filler plus a wire brush and caulk gun; $50-150 for a larger driveway including a 5-gallon asphalt sealcoat pail ($20-40). Pro: roughly $100-600 for crack repair and/or sealcoating a typical driveway; slab leveling (mudjacking/polyurethane foam) about $500-1,300; concrete section replacement $1,500-5,000+ depending on size.
timeEstimate: About 2-4 hours of active work for a typical driveway (more if you sealcoat), plus 24-48 hours of cure time before driving on it.
safetyNote: This is ground-level work with no electrical, gas, or height hazards, so no shutoffs are needed — but two hazards make it more than trivial. First, dust: chiseling or grinding concrete throws respirable crystalline silica, a serious known lung and cancer hazard (OSHA-regulated), not just a nuisance — wear a NIOSH-rated N95 or P100 mask, wet the area or use dust control when grinding, keep grinding to a minimum, and wear safety glasses. Second, hot-pour asphalt crack sealant runs 300°F or hotter and can cause serious burns — treat it as an advanced/pro method; if you use it, follow the melter's instructions exactly and never let a homeowner improvise it. Compressed air can fling debris, so keep glasses on and people/pets back. Wear gloves and eye protection with solvent-based fillers and sealants, work with ventilation, keep them away from flames/sparks (some are flammable), and read the product's safety data sheet. Don't work on a wet or freezing surface. If a crack shows a vertical step or the slab is sinking, that's a structural/base issue — stop and hire a professional rather than sealing over it.
toolsParts: NIOSH N95 or P100 dust mask
Cold chisel and hammer (or angle grinder with a crack-chasing blade for widening)
Screwdriver or putty knife for digging out debris/weeds
Shop vacuum, leaf blower, or compressed air
Garden hose or pressure washer for cleaning
Self-leveling polyurethane concrete crack sealant (for concrete)
Cold rubberized asphalt crack filler — bottle and/or trowel grade (for asphalt)
Trowel-grade concrete patch (for wider concrete cracks)
Putty knife or trowel for tooling
Driveway sealcoat and squeegee/brush (optional, asphalt only)
Rags and mineral spirits for cleanup
